# The Space Between Thoughts

I find myself thinking about gaps lately. Not the clothing store, though that's funny to consider—the actual spaces between things. The silence between words. The pause before you answer a question. The moment when you wake up and haven't remembered yet that you're supposed to be worried about something.

There's something profound about emptiness that we don't talk about enough. We're obsessed with filling things: filling time, filling silence, filling space. We scroll through our phones at red lights. We play music in the shower. We talk over the quiet parts of conversations because quiet feels dangerous somehow, like it might expose something we're not ready to admit.

But I've been noticing lately that the best moments are often the ones we're trying to skip over.

My grandmother sits on her porch in the evening and doesn't do anything. She just sits there. No phone, no book, no specific purpose. And when I asked her once if she was bored, she laughed—actually laughed—like I'd suggested the funniest thing. "Why would I be bored?" she asked. "There's so much to think about."

I didn't understand then. I do now, a little bit.

There's this strange pressure we're all under—I don't think I'm the only one who feels it—to be constantly productive. To be "on." To have a side hustle and a morning routine and a clearly defined personal brand. To be able to explain, at any moment, what we're working toward. There's this sense that if you're not moving forward, you're falling behind. That stillness is just laziness wearing a disguise.

But what if it's not?

What if sometimes the most important work is the thinking kind? The kind you can't point to or show anyone. The kind that happens in the shower, or on a walk, or in that blessed moment between sleep and waking.

I read something once about how some people are "comfortable with ambiguity." I think that's what I'm trying to get at. Some people can sit with questions and not immediately need an answer. Can be in the middle of something and not panic about how it ends. Can look at their life and say, "I don't know what this is yet," without that sentence feeling like a failure.

I'm trying to be more like that.

It's harder than it sounds. The voice in my head—maybe you have one too—is always narrating. Always evaluating. Is this a good use of time? Should I be doing something else? Am I behind? Am I enough? The questions form these little tight knots in your chest if you let them.

Sometimes I catch myself mid-worry about something that hasn't even happened yet. Mid-regret about something I can't change. And I think about those gaps again. How you can't actually live in the past or the future. How the only place you can actually exist is in this breath, this moment, this space right here.

This is not revolutionary information. Buddhist monks have known this for about three thousand years. But it's one thing to know something and another thing to feel it in your body.

I've been trying to practice it. Not even meditating—I'm too fidgety for formal meditation, at least so far. But just... noticing. When I'm eating, actually tasting it instead of shoveling and thinking about what comes next. When I'm with someone, actually looking at their face instead of planning what to say. When I'm walking, feeling my feet on the ground.

It's strange how radical these things feel.

There's this moment that happens almost every day where you get a notification—a text, an email, a notification from an app—and before you even read it, your nervous system is already activated. Your whole body is on standby waiting to react. And sometimes it's just someone asking if you want to grab lunch. But you've already gone through the entire emotional journey of possible catastrophe in the space of three seconds.

I wonder what that's doing to us, that constant state of alert. I wonder if we even know what regular peace feels like anymore.

Last week I was stuck in traffic and couldn't do anything about it. My phone died—it actually died, dramatic and completely. And at first I was anxious. But then something shifted. And I just sat there. I watched the clouds. I listened to the radio DJ's voice. I noticed that the woman in the car next to me was singing, and I didn't know the song but I could tell she knew every word by heart.

It was nice. Boring, by some measures. But actually nice.

I think we're going to look back on this time—this era of constant connectivity, constant pressure, constant awareness of everything happening everywhere to everyone—and think: how did they do that? How did they survive that? Didn't they want to just sit still sometimes?

The answer is yes. We did. We do. But we forgot it was allowed.

This is me remembering.

I'm not going to pretend I have it figured out. I'm still anxious about things that haven't happened. I still check my phone too much. I still sometimes feel that little surge of panic that everyone else knows something I don't, that life is a test I'm failing.

But I'm trying to spend more time in the gaps. In the spaces between productivity and purpose. In the actual present moment, which is the only one that's real.

And maybe that's enough. Maybe that's the whole thing.

Sit on your porch. Taste your food. Look at someone's face while they're talking. Let yourself think without immediately demanding an answer.

The world will still be there when you're done. It will probably be on fire about something. But you'll be more ready for it if you took a moment first.
